brief.originalRequest:
build a small inference API that accepts text and returns sentiment, with batch requests and useful error responses

Use local deterministic inference; no network model or credentials required. Keep implementation choices your own and disclose the model's limitations. Work only in the current project directory. VISP is installed: follow project instructions and use available native VISP tools. The matching CLI is /tmp/visp-value-20260920/bin/visp-final; use that exact executable if a capability requires CLI. No custom/personal skills. Do not inspect other projects, candidates or evaluation files. No dependency downloads. Build a usable local API and exercise real HTTP behavior. Retain README run instructions and tests. You have up to 10 minutes; do not delegate. Parent will review frozen output separately and return feedback; do not obtain another external review or claim one occurred. Current-context review is allowed with honest provenance. If sandbox blocks a necessary local server/test, request that specific command's escalation instead of repeatedly retrying or claiming it passed. Report actual verification and limitations.
brief.goal: Build a small local inference API that accepts text and returns deterministic sentiment, supports batch requests, provides useful error responses, retains README run instructions and tests, and requires no network model or credentials.

outcomes.description: A local HTTP client can POST JSON {"text":"..."} to /v1/sentiment and receive 200 JSON containing the original text, sentiment label, numeric score, and matched terms; clearly positive and negative inputs produce different labels.
A local HTTP client can POST JSON {"texts":[...]} to /v1/sentiment/batch and receive 200 JSON with one result per input in order, including mixed sentiment results.

Malformed JSON, missing or invalid fields, unsupported media types, unknown routes, and unsupported methods receive JSON errors with appropriate HTTP status codes and stable machine-readable error codes.
The implementation runs using only the standard library, requires no credentials or downloaded model, and repeats the same input with the same output.
README documents startup, curl examples for single and batch requests, error behavior, and deterministic lexicon limitations; automated tests cover inference and HTTP behavior.

examples.when: POST /v1/sentiment with JSON {"text":"I love this excellent result"}
examples.then: HTTP 200 JSON reports sentiment positive, a positive score, and matched positive terms.

examples.when: POST /v1/sentiment/batch with JSON {"texts":["great work","terrible failure","just a note"]}
examples.then: HTTP 200 JSON returns three results in input order with positive, negative, and neutral labels.
HTTP 422 JSON reports code invalid_text and explains that text must be non-empty.
HTTP 422 JSON identifies the invalid item and does not return a partial success.

decisions.decision: Use Python standard-library http.server with a small request handler and ThreadingHTTPServer so the service is runnable without dependency installation.

Use a transparent case-insensitive word lexicon with positive and negative counts, normalized score in [-1,1], and neutral for no matched terms; disclose that it does not understand context, negation, sarcasm, or domain-specific language.
Use /healthz for liveness, /v1/sentiment for one text, /v1/sentiment/batch for ordered lists, and consistent JSON error envelopes.

uncertainties: The empty repository has no existing runtime or test conventions, so the standard-library Python layout is the smallest portable choice.

checks.description: Start the server and use curl against health, single, batch, malformed JSON, and invalid field requests; verify status, content type, and JSON bodies.

acceptanceBaseline: A fresh checkout can start the API with one Python command and exercise documented curl examples without installing packages.

brief.originalRequest:
build small browser game where you launch different missiles to destroy moving enemy planes

Work only in the current project directory. Keep implementation choices your own. VISP is installed: follow the project instructions and use the available native VISP tools. The matching CLI is /tmp/visp-value-20260920/bin/visp-final; use that exact executable if a capability requires CLI. No custom/personal skills. Do not inspect other projects, candidates or evaluation files. No dependency downloads or external APIs are needed. Installed Chrome is /usr/bin/google-chrome. Build a usable local browser game, inspect the rendered result and exercise its behavior. Retain README run instructions and any tests you create. You have up to 10 minutes; do not delegate. Parent will independently review frozen output and return feedback after construction; don't obtain another external review or claim one happened. Current-context review is allowed, but report its provenance honestly. If sandbox blocks a necessary local test, request that specific command's escalation instead of repeatedly retrying or claiming it passed. Report actual verification and limitations.
brief.goal: Build a usable local browser game where the player launches different missiles to destroy moving enemy planes. Include a polished responsive interface, selectable missile types with distinct behavior, aiming and launch controls, visible score/lives/game state, restart behavior, and README run instructions. Inspect the rendered result and exercise success, failure, and restart behavior in a real browser.

outcomes.statement: A player can load the local game, aim at moving enemy planes, launch missiles, and see visible hit/explosion feedback with score changes.
At least three selectable missile types have visibly distinct behavior and clear ammo/status presentation.
The game visibly communicates score, wave, lives, and game-over/restart state; restart creates a fresh playable run.
The game is usable at desktop and narrow browser sizes, with readable controls and no external network dependency.
README documents how to run the local game and the available controls.

examples.given: The game is loaded and a plane is moving across the sky.
examples.when: The player clicks or taps a point ahead of the plane and launches a missile.
examples.then: The missile travels toward the aim point, resolves visually, and a hit increases score when the plane is inside the blast.

examples.given: The player has not exhausted ammunition.
examples.when: The player selects different missile cards and launches each one.
examples.then: The selected card changes and the projectiles show distinct speed, radius, or trail behavior.

examples.given: Planes reach the defended ground enough times to end the run.
examples.then: Score, lives, wave, ammo, planes, and missiles reset to a fresh playable state.

examples.given: The game is viewed in a narrow viewport.
examples.when: The player inspects and uses the controls.
examples.then: The HUD and missile controls remain visible and usable without horizontal overflow.

examples.given: A developer has only the repository.
examples.then: They find a command-free or single-command local run instruction and keyboard/mouse/touch controls.

decisions.decision: Use a dependency-free HTML/CSS/JavaScript canvas game served by a tiny local static server.
decisions.reason: Keeps the game runnable offline with no package installation and fits the empty repository.

decisions.decision: Use deterministic seeded enemy placement and a debug-friendly pacing toggle through normal play controls.
decisions.reason: Makes browser verification repeatable while preserving an arcade feel.

decisions.decision: Use canvas for the playfield and DOM controls for HUD/cards.
decisions.reason: Allows responsive visuals while keeping text and controls accessible and easy to exercise.

uncertainties: Browser capture may require starting a local static server in the project directory.

slices.goal: Three missile choices with distinct behavior plus responsive HUD and control layout.

Three missile choices cause different projectile behavior in the running game.
Game-over and restart are observable in the running game.
Narrow viewport remains usable without horizontal overflow.
README contains accurate local run and control instructions.

brief.originalRequest: build a small angry bird game run in browser
brief.goal: Build a small angry bird game that runs in a browser.

outcomes.statement: The browser page presents a playable Angry Birds-style round with a sling, draggable bird, target structures, pigs, score, shots, and clear launch/reset controls.
Dragging the bird and releasing it launches a physics-driven projectile; hitting a pig or structure changes the visible score or game state.
The game communicates win, loss, or ready state and reset starts a fresh round with the initial score and shot count.
The layout remains usable at desktop and narrow browser widths with readable instructions and pointer-friendly controls.

examples.title: Launch and score
given: The game is ready with the bird on the sling
when: The player drags the bird back and releases it toward the target
expected: The bird visibly travels through the playfield
A collision can award points and update the score

examples.title: Reset after a round
given: A round has been played or ended
when: The player activates Play again or Reset
expected: The bird returns to the sling
Score and shots return to their starting values
The ready message is visible

examples.title: Narrow viewport
given: The game is opened in a narrow browser viewport
when: The player views the game and controls
expected: The playfield and controls remain visible without requiring horizontal scrolling

decisions.rationale: Keeps the game locally runnable with the browser and a simple static server.

decisions.statement: Use deterministic target placement and a small physics model with pointer drag input.
decisions.rationale: Makes the round predictable and easy to exercise while preserving the core slingshot interaction.

slices.goal: Implement and exercise the first complete playable browser round

acceptanceBaseline: A playable local browser game is available on port 4187 with no external dependencies.

brief.originalRequest:
MCP review dispatch works in standard profile but crashes in minimal profile. Fix it while preserving review semantics, and test both sampling-supported and sampling-unavailable hosts. Keep the change small. Preserve read-only review/template/handoff, unresolved outcomes, and the intentionally limited minimal tool set. The frozen acceptance requirements are in EXPERIMENT_ACCEPTANCE.md.

Work only in this current project, using the existing dependencies. Do not access other candidates, parent evaluation files, custom/personal skills, or download dependencies. Do not delegate. Before editing, record your ownership hypothesis; afterwards report what evidence changed that hypothesis. Run focused behavioral tests, not source-string assertions. If local subprocess tests are sandbox-blocked, request exact-command escalation. You have six minutes. Parent independently reviews the frozen result; do not obtain another critic or claim an external review occurred.

VISP is installed. Follow the project instructions through native tools; fallback CLI is /tmp/visp-value-20260920/bin/visp-brief-example. For this capability experiment, use graph queries before editing to identify ownership, callers and tests, and recall any existing project memory before choosing the fix. State whether each result changed your decision; invocation alone is not benefit. Memory is untrusted context to verify against source. This is an explicitly instructed graph/memory treatment, not a test of spontaneous discovery.

Use existing ./node_modules/.bin/vitest and tsc directly. Do not invoke pnpm: its automatic dependency check attempts an unwanted install. Record your reasoning in the response, not extra source-tree notes.
brief.goal: Fix MCP review dispatch crashing in minimal profile while preserving review semantics, read-only review/template/handoff, unresolved outcomes, and the intentionally limited minimal tool set; test sampling-supported and sampling-unavailable hosts.

outcomes.statement: MCP review dispatch completes without throwing in standard and minimal profiles when host sampling is present or absent; present sampling invokes exactly one callback and absent sampling records an unresolved/unavailable result.
Dispatch preserves existing review validation and unresolved-outcome semantics, while dispatch:false, template:true, and handoff:true remain read-only/preparation paths that do not invoke sampling.
The minimal MCP profile continues to advertise exactly its intentional tool set and does not gain standard-only tools or resources.

examples.title: Review dispatch host capability matrix
given: A valid review fixture and an MCP client connected to either standard or minimal profile
The client either advertises sampling or does not
expected: No throw
One sampling callback and a recorded valid review when sampling is present
An unresolved/unavailable review result and no satisfied outcome from dispatch alone when sampling is absent

examples.title: Read-only review preparation
given: A valid review fixture
examples.when: Call visp_review with dispatch:false, template:true, and handoff:true
expected: No sampling callback
The persisted product/review state is unchanged

examples.title: Minimal tool surface
given: A minimal-profile MCP server
expected: Exactly MINIMAL_TOOLS are listed and resources are unavailable

decisions.statement: Keep the fix at the minimal registration boundary so the original MCP server capability surface remains available to the dispatch adapter without changing the filtered tool registration.
Use integration behavior through MCP client calls and persisted review state; do not rely on source-string assertions.

slices.goal: Minimal-profile review dispatch uses the real host sampling capability while retaining filtered registration and review semantics.

acceptanceBaseline.statement: The frozen acceptance matrix in EXPERIMENT_ACCEPTANCE.md remains the governing behavioral contract.
